definition: Painstaking means taking great pains or care; extremely thorough and careful.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word painstaking. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know painstaking should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Reassembling the shattered vase was painstaking work that took the conservator an entire month.
Careful is the everyday baseline — you can be careful in a minute; painstaking implies sustained, effortful care over every detail of a demanding task.
Obsessive goes beyond painstaking into unhealthy territory, where the attention to detail no longer serves the work at all.

Meticulous describes extreme, exacting care over small details — a standard the finished work meets, however easily the care comes. Painstaking praises the effort itself: the pains taken, the hours spent getting details right. Work can be meticulous without struggle, but nothing is painstaking unless real labor went in.

Thorough means complete in coverage — nothing skipped, every part dealt with. Painstaking is about the intensity of care and effort poured into the details, not mere coverage. A checklist can make you thorough; only sustained, effortful attention makes a job painstaking.

For seventy years, volunteers mailed slips of paper to a shed in Oxford, each slip recording one word found in one book.
James Murray, the dictionary's first editor, sorted the slips by hand into thousands of pigeonholes, tracing how every meaning of every word had shifted across the centuries.
The work was painstaking in the plainest sense: a single entry could swallow a week, and the letter A alone took years to finish.
Colleagues urged him to hurry, to skim, to settle for the obvious senses.
Murray refused; each quotation was checked against its source before it was allowed in.
He did not live to see the final volume.
But the effort he poured into the details, hour by hour, is why the dictionary is still trusted today.
